title: Shallow and deep copies
summary: Why copying a list of lists still shares the inner lists, and when copy.deepcopy is the right tool.

blocks.html: You build a 3x2 grid with grid = [[None] * 2] * 3, set grid[0][0] = 5, and the first cell of every row changes. The Python FAQ lists exactly this as a common trap [FAQ]. Another time you carefully copied a configuration with .copy() and edited the copy, and the original still changed. Both bugs share one cause.

config.title: Does the change leak back into a?
config.intro: Each snippet starts with a = [[1], [2]] and then runs the code shown. Decide whether printing a afterwards shows a change. Predict first.

items.feedback: The slice is a new outer list, but b[0] is the same inner list as a[0]. Local run: a is [[1, 9], [2]].
append changes the outer list of b only, which is separate from a's. Local run: a is [[1], [2]].
Item assignment on b rebinds a slot in b's own outer list. a's slot is untouched.
deepcopy copies the inner lists too.
list(a) is a shallow copy; b[0] and a[0] are one object. Local run: a is [[7], [2]].
Each inner list was copied, so nothing is shared.

config.debrief: The rule: a shallow copy shares every item it holds. Changes that replace or add items in the outer list stay local; changes that mutate a shared inner object leak.

blocks.instructions: Sort every snippet, and say for each one which object is shared.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed the dividing line: does the change mutate an inner object that both lists hold?

blocks.html: A shallow copy is like photocopying the table of contents of a filing cabinet: you now hold your own list of drawers, but every entry still points at the same physical folders. A deep copy is photocopying the folders too.
blocks.limits: Real photocopies do not create live references. In Python a shallow copy genuinely holds references to the original items, so mutating a shared item is visible from both containers, while replacing an item in one container is not. Also, deep copy is not always desirable (see the explanation).

blocks.purpose: Show which objects a shallow and a deep copy share with the original.
blocks.alt: Three stacked diagrams of the list [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. The original has an outer list pointing to inner lists A and B. A shallow copy has a new outer list whose arrows point to the same A and B. A deep copy has a new outer list pointing to new inner lists A prime and B prime.

blocks.title: Definitions, tools and the limits of deepcopy
blocks.html:
The copy module defines the terms precisely: a shallow copy constructs a new compound object and then (to the extent possible) inserts references into it to the objects found in the original; a deep copy constructs a new compound object and then, recursively, inserts copies of the objects found in the original [copy module].

For a list, the built-in ways of making a shallow copy are s.copy(), which the docs say is equivalent to s[:] [sequence types], and the module-level copy.copy(s). I also use list(s); not verified in the docs I read as a listed copy idiom, but I confirmed locally that it makes a new outer list sharing the items.

orig = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
sh = orig.copy(); dp = copy.deepcopy(orig)
orig[0].append(99)
print(orig)   # [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]
print(sh)     # [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]   inner list shared
print(dp)     # [[1, 2], [3, 4]]       independent
print(orig is sh, [i is j for i, j in zip(orig, sh)])  # False [True, True]

The same mechanism produces the grid trap. The FAQ explains that replicating a list with * does not create copies, only references to the existing objects [FAQ]; the library reference gives the same warning for [[]] * 3 [sequence types]. The fix is a comprehension that builds a new inner list per row.

A = [[None] * 2] * 3
A[0][0] = 5
print(A)  # [[5, None], [5, None], [5, None]]
B = [[None] * 2 for _ in range(3)]
B[0][0] = 5
print(B)  # [[5, None], [None, None], [None, None]]

When not to deep-copy. The documentation lists two problems: recursive objects may cause a recursive loop (deepcopy handles this with a memo of what it already copied), and because deep copy copies everything it may copy too much, such as data intended to be shared between copies [copy module]. Simplification: for this course, copying means lists of lists and dictionaries of lists; user-defined classes can customise copying, which is out of scope.

blocks.title: Fix a copied configuration
blocks.html:
Goal: make a variant of cfg with an extra tag, leaving cfg untouched. Outputs from a local python3 run.

cfg = {'tags': ['a'], 'opts': {'v': 1}}
c1 = cfg.copy()
c1['tags'].append('b')
print(cfg)

steps.html: cfg.copy() is a shallow copy: a new dict, same values. c1['tags'] is the same list as cfg['tags'].
Only tags is mutated, so you could copy just that: c1['tags'] = cfg['tags'] + ['b']. This avoids copying opts needlessly.

blocks.result: Decision rule: copy at the depth at which you will mutate. Shallow suffices if you only replace top-level items; deep if you mutate nested ones; a targeted copy if only one part changes.

blocks.prompt:
Predict the output.
m = [1, [2, 3]]
m2 = m[:]
m2[0] = 10
m2[1][0] = 20
print(m)

feedback.0: This assumes the slice is a fully independent copy. Item 1 is a shared inner list.
feedback.1: m2[0] = 10 rebinds a slot in m2's own outer list; m is not affected.
feedback.3: Reversed: slot 0 is not shared, the inner list is.

blocks.explanation: The outer list is new, so replacing slot 0 stays local, but m[1] and m2[1] are the same inner list, so item assignment through it leaks. Local run output: [1, [20, 3]].

blocks.task:
Fix the grid builder so that setting one cell changes only that cell. Predict the buggy output first; run both in your Python.

def build_grid(n):
    row = [0] * n
    return [row] * n

G = build_grid(3)
G[1][1] = 7
print(G)
hints: How many distinct list objects are in the grid?
You need a new row object on every iteration.
rubric: My fix creates a new row for each row
I verified in my own Python
blocks.solution: Buggy output (local run): [[0, 7, 0], [0, 7, 0], [0, 7, 0]]. Fix: return [[0] * n for _ in range(n)], giving [[0, 0, 0], [0, 7, 0], [0, 0, 0]].

blocks.task: Build a three-level structure (a list containing a dict that contains a list). Make a shallow copy and a deep copy. Mutate the innermost list through the original, predict what each copy shows, then verify with is and by printing. Finally write one sentence on a case where deepcopy would copy too much.
rubric: Used is on at least one inner object to show sharing
Shallow copy leaks, deep copy does not

blocks.model: The shallow copy shows the mutated inner list; the deep copy does not. deepcopy copies too much when the structure holds something that should stay shared, such as a reference to a shared configuration or cache; the docs describe this problem [copy module].

questions.prompt: What is a shallow copy of a list?
options: A new list holding references to the same items
A new list holding copies of every item
The same list under a new name
A list with only the first level of items

feedback.3: A shallow copy has all the items; it just does not copy them.

questions.explanation: Definition from the copy module [copy module].

questions.prompt: a = [[1], [2]]; b = a.copy(); b[0] = [5]. What is a?

feedback.1: This replaces slot 0 of b's own outer list; it does not mutate the shared inner list.

questions.explanation: Replacing an element of the copy changes only the copy. Compare with b[0][0] = 5, which would leak.

questions.prompt: Why is [[0] * 3] * 3 risky but [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)] safe?
options: * repeats the same inner list; the comprehension builds a new one each time

feedback.2: The comprehension just evaluates [0]*3 afresh each iteration.
feedback.3: They differ, as the FAQ example shows.

questions.explanation: [FAQ] Replication with * creates references to existing objects, not copies.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words when a shallow copy is enough and when you need a deep copy.
rubric: Shallow is enough when items are immutable or are only replaced
Deep is needed when nested mutable items will be mutated
Mentions that deepcopy can copy too much
questions.model: A shallow copy suffices when items are immutable or you only replace/add top-level items. Use a deep copy when you will mutate nested mutable objects and need independence, remembering it may copy data meant to be shared [copy module].

blocks.task: A function keeps a history for an undo feature: history.append(state) where state is a dict containing lists of selected items. After several edits, all history entries show the latest selection. Explain why, decide between a shallow copy, a deep copy or restructuring, and justify the choice with the cost of each.
rubric: Explains that every history entry is the same object (or shares inner lists)
Distinguishes appending the same state from appending a copy
Chooses a copy depth and justifies it
Mentions that deepcopy may copy too much or cost memory
blocks.model: history.append(state) stores a reference to the one mutable state, so later edits show in every entry. Store a copy. A shallow copy is enough if you replace lists instead of mutating them; if code mutates the nested lists, use copy.deepcopy(state) (or store immutable tuples). Deep copies cost memory and time per entry and could duplicate data meant to be shared, so copy only what changes if the state is large [copy module].
